claim: LC spiking consistently preceded S1 membrane potential depolarization in mice performing a tactile detection task.
source: While LC spiking consistently preceded S1 membrane potential depolarization and pupil dilation, the correlation between S1 and pupil was more heterogeneous.
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis showing LC spikes preceded S1 depolarization with time lags of 0.17 ± 0.06 s (Figure 3a-c).

claim: LC spiking consistently preceded pupil dilation in mice performing a tactile detection task.
source: While LC spiking consistently preceded S1 membrane potential depolarization and pupil dilation, the correlation between S1 and pupil was more heterogeneous.
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis showing LC spikes preceded pupil dilation with time lags of 1.89 ± 0.25 s (Figure 3d-f).

claim: The correlation between S1 and pupil was more heterogeneous than the correlations between LC and S1 or LC and pupil.
source: While LC spiking consistently preceded S1 membrane potential depolarization and pupil dilation, the correlation between S1 and pupil was more heterogeneous.
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis showing heterogeneous correlations with both positive and negative correlations and time lags (Figure 3g-i).

claim: The relationships between LC, S1, and pupil varied on timescales of sub-seconds to seconds within trials.
source: Furthermore, the relationships between LC, S1, and pupil varied on timescales of sub-seconds to seconds within trials.
evidence: Supported by task epoch-dependent analysis showing different correlations during tone, stimulus, lick, and quiet periods (Figure 4).

claim: Pupil diameter can be dissociated from LC spiking.
source: Our data suggest that pupil diameter can be dissociated from LC spiking and cannot be used as a stationary index of LC activity.
evidence: Supported by epoch-dependent analysis showing different response profiles for LC and pupil across task events (Figure 4).

claim: Pupil diameter cannot be used as a stationary index of LC activity.
source: Our data suggest that pupil diameter can be dissociated from LC spiking and cannot be used as a stationary index of LC activity.
evidence: Supported by non-stationary correlations between LC and pupil that depend on task epoch (Figure 4).

claim: LC activity modulates feedforward processing of sensory stimuli.
source: First, LC activity modulates feedforward processing of sensory stimuli (Hirata et al., 2006; Devilbiss et al., 2006; Rodenkirch et al., 2019) and impacts sensory cortex states (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Polack et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC activity impacts sensory cortex states.
source: First, LC activity modulates feedforward processing of sensory stimuli (Hirata et al., 2006; Devilbiss et al., 2006; Rodenkirch et al., 2019) and impacts sensory cortex states (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Polack et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC activity correlates with task performance.
source: Second, LC activity correlates with task performance (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Usher et al., 1999) and pupil diameter (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC activity correlates with pupil diameter.
source: Second, LC activity correlates with task performance (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Usher et al., 1999) and pupil diameter (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and data from this study showing correlation coefficient of 0.15 ± 0.02 (Figure 2b).

claim: Pupil diameter is thought to index arousal.
source: Finally, pupil diameter is thought to index arousal and has been found to be correlated with neuronal and behavioral detection or discrimination sensitivity (Reimer et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Vinck et al., 2015; Lee and Margolis, 2016; Schriver et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Cazettes et al., 2021), as well as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pupil diameter has been found to be correlated with neuronal and behavioral detection or discrimination sensitivity.
source: Finally, pupil diameter is thought to index arousal and has been found to be correlated with neuronal and behavioral detection or discrimination sensitivity (Reimer et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Vinck et al., 2015; Lee and Margolis, 2016; Schriver et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Cazettes et al., 2021), as well as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pupil diameter has been found to be correlated with decision bias.
source: Finally, pupil diameter is thought to index arousal and has been found to be correlated with neuronal and behavioral detection or discrimination sensitivity (Reimer et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Vinck et al., 2015; Lee and Margolis, 2016; Schriver et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Cazettes et al., 2021), as well as decision bias (de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sensory cortex activity impacts perceptual reports.
source: Since sensory cortex activity impacts perceptual reports (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Miyashita and Feldman, 2013), these observations suggest the hypothesis that LC/NE modulates sensory cortex activity and affects perceptual task performance and that this effect can be monitored noninvasively via the easy-to-measure pupil diameter.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC/NE modulates sensory cortex activity and affects perceptual task performance.
source: Since sensory cortex activity impacts perceptual reports (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Miyashita and Feldman, 2013), these observations suggest the hypothesis that LC/NE modulates sensory cortex activity and affects perceptual task performance and that this effect can be monitored noninvasively via the easy-to-measure pupil diameter.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on logical inference from cited literature.

claim: LC spiking activity and pupil diameter were correlated across entire sessions with a peak correlation coefficient of 0.15 ± 0.02.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), cross-correlogram analysis revealed that LC spiking activity and pupil diameter were correlated across entire sessions, with pupil dilation following LC spikes (peak correlation coefficient: 0.15 ± 0.02; time lags: 2.61 ± 0.39 s, n = 39 recordings, Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis of experimental data (Figure 2b).

claim: Pupil dilation followed LC spikes with time lags of 2.61 ± 0.39 s.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), cross-correlogram analysis revealed that LC spiking activity and pupil diameter were correlated across entire sessions, with pupil dilation following LC spikes (peak correlation coefficient: 0.15 ± 0.02; time lags: 2.61 ± 0.39 s, n = 39 recordings, Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis of experimental data (Figure 2b).

claim: Mean LC spiking activity showed prominent responses to a tone delivered at the beginning of each trial.
source: Mean LC spiking activity aligned with trial onsets showed prominent responses to a tone delivered at the beginning of each trial, as well as in trials where mice made Go (licking) responses (Hit and False Alarm trials, Figure 2a,c).
evidence: Supported by trial-aligned LC spike rate data (Figure 2a,c).

claim: Mean LC spiking activity showed prominent responses in trials where mice made Go (licking) responses.
source: Mean LC spiking activity aligned with trial onsets showed prominent responses to a tone delivered at the beginning of each trial, as well as in trials where mice made Go (licking) responses (Hit and False Alarm trials, Figure 2a,c).
evidence: Supported by trial-aligned LC spike rate data (Figure 2a,c).

claim: LC spiking activity to the tone was comparable to Go responses (p=0.24).
source: LC spiking activity to the tone was comparable to Go responses (p=0.24, Figure 2d, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of LC responses (Figure 2d).

claim: Pre-stimulus LC activity was slightly but significantly lower on Hit trials compared to Miss trials.
source: On Hit trials, where mice successfully licked to the whisker stimulus, pre-stimulus LC activity (measured in a 0.5 s window prior to stimulus onset) was slightly but significantly lower than Miss trials, where mice failed to lick to the whisker stimulus (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison showing p=0.0083 (Figure 2e).

claim: On Miss trials, LC responded weakly to the whisker stimulus alone (<0.5 sp/s above baseline).
source: We note that on Miss trials, LC responded weakly to the whisker stimulus alone (<0.5 sp/s above baseline, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LC activity measured in a short window (0.2 s) after stimulus onset was larger on Hits compared with Misses.
source: LC activity measured in a short window (0.2 s) after stimulus onset was larger on Hits compared with Misses (Figure 2e; the same trend holds for 0.1 s window, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison showing p=5.5e-7 (Figure 2e).

claim: Pre-stimulus LC activity significantly predicted perceptual reports of the mice on a trial-by-trial basis with a choice probability of 0.47 ± 0.014 (p=0.032).
source: Ideal-observer analysis showed that both pre- and post-stimulus LC activity significantly predicted perceptual reports of the mice on a trial-by-trial basis, with choice probabilities (Yang et al., 2016) of 0.47 ± 0.014 (p=0.032, n = 43) for pre-stimulus and 0.59 ± 0.017 (p=4.6e-6, n = 43) for post-stimulus LC activity, respectively (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by ideal-observer analysis of experimental data (Figure 2e).

claim: Post-stimulus LC activity significantly predicted perceptual reports of the mice on a trial-by-trial basis with a choice probability of 0.59 ± 0.017 (p=4.6e-6).
source: Ideal-observer analysis showed that both pre- and post-stimulus LC activity significantly predicted perceptual reports of the mice on a trial-by-trial basis, with choice probabilities (Yang et al., 2016) of 0.47 ± 0.014 (p=0.032, n = 43) for pre-stimulus and 0.59 ± 0.017 (p=4.6e-6, n = 43) for post-stimulus LC activity, respectively (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by ideal-observer analysis of experimental data (Figure 2e).

claim: LC spiking responses began ~200 ms prior to licking.
source: LC activity aligned to the time of licking showed that spiking responses began ~200 ms prior to licking (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by lick-aligned LC spike rate data (Figure 2f).

claim: Pupil diameter minimally increased in response to the tone.
source: In striking contrast, pupil diameter minimally increased in response to the tone.
evidence: Supported by pupil diameter measurements shown in Figure 2a,c,d.

claim: Pupil strongly dilated on Hit and False Alarm trials, in which mice made Go (licking) responses.
source: Instead, pupil strongly dilated on Hit and False Alarm trials, in which mice made Go (licking) responses (Figure 2a,c,d; tone vs. Go: p=6.4e-5, n = 36, Materials and methods) (Lee and Margolis, 2016).
evidence: Supported by pupil diameter measurements and statistical comparison (Figure 2a,c,d).

claim: Pupil response to the tone was larger on Misses compared to Hits.
source: Interestingly, pupil response to the tone was larger on Misses compared to Hits and significantly predicted perceptual choices of the mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pupil response to the tone significantly predicted perceptual choices of the mice.
source: Interestingly, pupil response to the tone was larger on Misses compared to Hits and significantly predicted perceptual choices of the mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by choice probability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pupil responses occurred after licking.
source: Pupil diameter changes (∆Pupil) aligned to the time of licking showed that pupil responses occurred after licking (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by lick-aligned pupil diameter data (Figure 2f).

claim: LC activity and pupil diameter appear to reflect different sets of task events during this behavior.
source: Thus, LC activity and pupil diameter appear to reflect different sets of task events during this behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the different response profiles of LC and pupil to tone and licking events.

claim: LC spikes were associated with a depolarization in cortical neurons (1.39 ± 0.35 mV, n = 12).
source: LC spike-triggered Vm analyses revealed that LC spikes were associated with a depolarization in cortical neurons (1.39 ± 0.35 mV, n = 12, Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 3a-c).

claim: Vm depolarization associated with an LC spike peaked after the spike, with short time lags of 0.17 ± 0.06 s.
source: On average, Vm depolarization associated with an LC spike peaked after the spike, with short time lags from an LC spike to peak depolarization in S1 (0.17 ± 0.06 s, n = 12, Figure 3a–c; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 3a-c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Pupil diameter increased in association with individual spikes from LC single units (0.03 ± 0.01 mm, n = 7).
source: Consistent with the previous cross-correlogram analysis based on a larger set of LC–pupil recordings (Figure 2b), here STA analysis showed that pupil diameter increased in association with individual spikes from LC single units (0.03 ± 0.01 mm, n = 7), with peak dilation occurring roughly 10-fold slower than peak Vm depolarization (time lags from an LC spike to peak pupil dilation: 1.89 ± 0.25 s, n = 7, Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 3d-f).

claim: Peak pupil dilation occurred roughly 10-fold slower than peak Vm depolarization.
source: Consistent with the previous cross-correlogram analysis based on a larger set of LC–pupil recordings (Figure 2b), here STA analysis showed that pupil diameter increased in association with individual spikes from LC single units (0.03 ± 0.01 mm, n = 7), with peak dilation occurring roughly 10-fold slower than peak Vm depolarization (time lags from an LC spike to peak pupil dilation: 1.89 ± 0.25 s, n = 7, Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of time lags: 1.89 s for pupil vs 0.17 s for Vm.

claim: Cross-correlogram analyses revealed heterogeneous correlations between pupil diameter and S1 Vm, with both positive and negative correlations as well as positive and negative time lags.
source: Cross-correlogram analyses revealed heterogeneous correlations between pupil diameter and S1 Vm, with both positive and negative correlations as well as positive and negative time lags (peak correlation coefficient: 0.05 ± 0.04; time lags: −0.22 ± 1.01 s, n = 19, Figure 3g–i).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis (Figure 3g-i).

claim: The time derivative of pupil diameter (pupil') was positively correlated with S1 Vm in a more consistent manner (peak correlation coefficient: 0.15 ± 0.03; time lags: 1.31 ± 0.24 s, n = 19).
source: In sharp contrast, the time derivative of pupil diameter (pupil') was positively correlated with S1 Vm in a more consistent manner (peak correlation coefficient: 0.15 ± 0.03; time lags: 1.31 ± 0.24 s, n = 19, Figure 3j,k; Reimer et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis (Figure 3j,k) and consistent with prior research.

claim: LC activity was superior in predicting cortical dynamics faster than ~200–300 ms.
source: We found that LC activity was superior in predicting cortical dynamics faster than ~200–300 ms (exponential decay time constant: LC–Vm vs. Pupil–Vm vs. Pupil'-Vm, 1.02 ± 0.09 vs. 6.59 ± 0.60 vs. 1.53 ± 0.14, Figure 3l; repeated-measures ANOVA, F(2, 36)=74.5, p=1.6e-13, n = 19).
evidence: Supported by high-pass filtering analysis and statistical comparison (Figure 3l).

claim: LC activity reflects higher frequency correlations with Vm compared with the pupil.
source: Post hoc Tukey–Kramer tests revealed that LC activity reflects higher frequency correlations with Vm compared with the pupil (LC–Vm vs. Pupil–Vm, p=5.9e-8; LC-Vm vs. Pupil'–Vm, p=0.0037; Pupil–Vm vs. Pupil'–Vm, p=7.1e-7).
evidence: Supported by post hoc statistical tests on high-pass filtering analysis.

claim: The LC–Pupil' relationship was similar to that of LC–Pupil.
source: On the other hand, the LC–Pupil' relationship was similar to that of LC–Pupil (compare Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with Figure 3e,f).
evidence: Supported by comparison of data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with Figure 3e,f.

claim: LC spikes preceded S1 depolarizations and pupil dilations.
source: Together, these data show that LC spikes preceded S1 depolarizations and pupil dilations.
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analyses showing positive time lags.

claim: LC spiking correlated with both Vm and pupil diameter changes, but on vastly different timescales (~0.2 s vs. ~2 s).
source: LC spiking correlated with both Vm and pupil diameter changes, but on vastly different timescales (~0.2 s vs. ~2 s).
evidence: Supported by time lag measurements from spike-triggered average analyses.

claim: The time derivative of pupil diameter, but not the absolute pupil size, is a good predictor of S1 Vm fluctuations.
source: Our data also show that the time derivative of pupil diameter, but not the absolute pupil size, is a good predictor of S1 Vm fluctuations.
evidence: Supported by comparison of correlation coefficients between pupil-Vm and pupil'-Vm (Figure 3g-k).

claim: LC spiking can track fast Vm fluctuations better than either pupil or pupil'.
source: However, LC spiking can track fast Vm fluctuations better than either pupil or pupil'.
evidence: Supported by high-pass filtering analysis showing LC has the slowest decay time constant (Figure 3l).

claim: Vm depolarization associated with an LC spike had the biggest response to tone/licking and almost no response during the quiet periods.
source: While single LC spikes were associated with prominent changes in both cortical Vm and pupil diameter, we found that these associations strikingly depended on task epoch: Vm depolarization associated with an LC spike had the biggest response to tone/licking and almost no response during the quiet periods (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by epoch-dependent spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 4a).

claim: Pupil dilation associated with an LC spike had the biggest response to licking and almost no response to the tone.
source: In contrast, pupil dilation associated with an LC spike had the biggest response to licking and almost no response to the tone (Figure 4b; this was true as well for pupil dilation after z-scoring, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by epoch-dependent spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The pupil' associated with an LC spike had an intermediate response to the tone.
source: The pupil' associated with an LC spike had an intermediate response to the tone (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by epoch-dependent spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 4c).

claim: Peak pupil dilation, pupil' and Vm depolarization appeared to have different dependencies on LC spike counts.
source: In addition, peak pupil dilation, pupil' and Vm depolarization appeared to have different dependencies on LC spike counts, with a roughly monotonic relationship between pupil and LC, and a much weaker dependence between Vm and LC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of responses as a function of LC spike counts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: The correlations between LC spiking and Vm, and between LC spiking and pupil diameter, are non-stationary, even on the timescale of a few seconds.
source: Thus, the correlations between LC spiking and Vm, and between LC spiking and pupil diameter, are non-stationary, even on the timescale of a few seconds.
evidence: Inferred from epoch-dependent differences in correlations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The correlations between LC activity and Vm and pupil each reflect distinct unmeasured underlying processes.
source: Importantly, these epoch dependencies were different for Vm and pupil – with the biggest response occurring to the tone for Vm and the smallest response occurring to the tone for pupil – suggesting that the correlations between LC activity and Vm and pupil each reflect distinct unmeasured underlying processes.
evidence: Inferred from the different epoch-dependent response patterns for Vm and pupil.

claim: Tonic LC activity is thought to reflect attentive state.
source: Tonic LC activity is thought to reflect attentive state (Usher et al., 1999; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pre-stimulus baseline LC spiking predicted behavioral responses.
source: We found that pre-stimulus baseline LC spiking predicted behavioral responses, suggesting that being in a hyperactive or distractable state underlies failed stimulus detection.
evidence: Supported by choice probability analysis showing significant prediction (Figure 2e).

claim: Being in a hyperactive or distractable state underlies failed stimulus detection.
source: We found that pre-stimulus baseline LC spiking predicted behavioral responses, suggesting that being in a hyperactive or distractable state underlies failed stimulus detection.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that higher baseline LC activity was associated with Miss trials.

claim: Higher baseline LC activity was correlated with more whisking, which has been shown to lead to failed stimulus detection.
source: However, it is possible that higher baseline LC activity was correlated with more whisking, which has been shown to lead to failed stimulus detection (Ollerenshaw et al., 2012; Kyriakatos et al., 2017).
evidence: Presented as a possible explanation with citations to prior research.

claim: Activating the LC–NE system enhances detection/discrimination sensitivity.
source: Recent optogenetic and pharmacological work has shown that activating the LC–NE system enhances detection/discrimination sensitivity (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018; Rodenkirch et al., 2019; McBurney-Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC–NE acting on early sensory areas likely affects perceptual decision making.
source: Thus, LC–NE acting on early sensory areas (i.e., primary sensory thalamus, primary sensory cortex) likely affects perceptual decision making (McBurney-Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from prior research with citation.

claim: S1 depolarizations immediately follow LC spiking.
source: We showed that S1 depolarizations immediately follow LC spiking, suggesting that LC activity at least partially contributes to the amount of depolarization in S1 neurons (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Polack et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis showing short time lags.

claim: LC activity at least partially contributes to the amount of depolarization in S1 neurons.
source: We showed that S1 depolarizations immediately follow LC spiking, suggesting that LC activity at least partially contributes to the amount of depolarization in S1 neurons (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Polack et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from temporal relationship between LC spikes and S1 depolarization, with citations to prior research.

claim: Sensory-evoked S1 responses predict the behavioral choices of the mice.
source: Given that sensory-evoked S1 responses predict the behavioral choices of the mice (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2016), our results suggest that the LC–S1 pathway is involved during this task.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The LC–S1 pathway is involved during this task.
source: Given that sensory-evoked S1 responses predict the behavioral choices of the mice (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2016), our results suggest that the LC–S1 pathway is involved during this task.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal relationship between LC and S1 activity and the role of S1 in behavioral choices.

claim: The effect could be mediated directly through LC innervation of S1 or indirectly through LC innervating other early somatosensory areas, such as the VPM thalamus.
source: However, the effect could be mediated directly through LC innervation of S1 or indirectly through LC innervating other early somatosensory areas, such as the VPM thalamus (Rodenkirch et al., 2019).
evidence: Presented as alternative possible mechanisms with citation.

claim: LC responded strongly to an auditory cue (tone) meant to alert the mice to the beginning of a trial.
source: LC responded strongly to an auditory cue (tone) meant to alert the mice to the beginning of a trial.
evidence: Supported by trial-aligned LC spike rate data (Figure 2a,c).

claim: LC responses to the auditory cue may be mediated via synaptic inputs to LC from the brainstem (e.g., nucleus paragigantocellularis).
source: Such responses may be mediated via synaptic inputs to LC from the brainstem (e.g., nucleus paragigantocellularis) (Ennis and Aston-Jones, 1988; Aston-Jones et al., 1991; Van Bockstaele et al., 1993; Llorca-Torralba et al., 2016).
evidence: Presented as a possible mechanism with citations to prior research.

claim: The robust LC spiking responses to the auditory cue are consistent with LC's role in promoting alertness or preparedness to detect a weak stimulus.
source: The robust LC spiking responses to this cue are therefore consistent with LC's role in promoting alertness or preparedness to detect a weak stimulus (Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: Inferred from the observed LC responses with citations to prior research on LC function.

claim: LC responded to operant licking responses.
source: We also found that LC responded to operant licking responses, which is consistent with earlier work showing that LC encoded overt decision execution (Kalwani et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by trial-aligned LC spike rate data (Figure 2a,c,f) and consistent with prior research.

claim: LC encoded overt decision execution.
source: We also found that LC responded to operant licking responses, which is consistent with earlier work showing that LC encoded overt decision execution (Kalwani et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: LC spiking and pupil diameter correlate well at long timescales.
source: Our data show that while LC spiking and pupil diameter correlate well at long timescales, and both can predict changes in cortical dynamics, LC does so an order of magnitude faster.
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis showing correlation at ~2 s timescale (Figure 2b).

claim: Both LC spiking and pupil diameter can predict changes in cortical dynamics.
source: Our data show that while LC spiking and pupil diameter correlate well at long timescales, and both can predict changes in cortical dynamics, LC does so an order of magnitude faster.
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analyses with S1 Vm (Figure 3).

claim: LC predicts changes in cortical dynamics an order of magnitude faster than pupil diameter.
source: Our data show that while LC spiking and pupil diameter correlate well at long timescales, and both can predict changes in cortical dynamics, LC does so an order of magnitude faster.
evidence: Supported by comparison of time lags: ~0.2 s for LC vs ~2 s for pupil.

claim: The correlation between pupil and Vm is much more heterogeneous than between LC and Vm.
source: Moreover, the correlation between pupil and Vm is much more heterogeneous than between LC and Vm.
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analyses showing variable correlations for pupil-Vm (Figure 3g-i) vs consistent correlations for LC-Vm (Figure 3a-c).

claim: Compared with change in the absolute size of pupil diameter, its time derivative is a better predictor of cortical states.
source: In support of previous studies, our results suggest that compared with change in the absolute size of pupil diameter, its time derivative is a better predictor of cortical states (Reimer et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison of correlation coefficients (Figure 3g-k) and consistent with prior research.

claim: The relationships between LC activity, S1 Vm, and pupil depended on task epoch.
source: Importantly, the relationships between LC activity, S1 Vm, and pupil depended on task epoch.
evidence: Supported by epoch-dependent spike-triggered average analysis (Figure 4).

claim: In attempting to use pupil diameter as a proxy for LC spiking, it would be useful to separately normalize distinct task epochs.
source: That is, in attempting to use pupil diameter as a proxy for LC spiking, our data suggest it would be useful to separately normalize distinct task epochs.
evidence: Inferred from the epoch-dependent differences in LC-pupil relationships.

claim: Pupil size changes have been linked to activity in multiple brain areas and neuromodulatory systems.
source: Pupil size changes have been linked to activity in multiple brain areas and neuromodulatory systems (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Cazettes et al., 2021), and different pupil response profiles reflect different cognitive processes (Schriver et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Different pupil response profiles reflect different cognitive processes.
source: Pupil size changes have been linked to activity in multiple brain areas and neuromodulatory systems (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Cazettes et al., 2021), and different pupil response profiles reflect different cognitive processes (Schriver et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The pupil exhibits dynamic coupling with different underlying brain circuits in a cognitive process (behavioral epoch)-dependent way.
source: Therefore, it is possible that the pupil exhibits dynamic coupling with different underlying brain circuits in a cognitive process (behavioral epoch)-dependent way.
evidence: Presented as a possible explanation for the observed epoch-dependent relationships.

claim: Pupil responses to dorsal raphe stimulation exhibited task uncertainty-dependent variations.
source: In addition, a recent study showed that pupil responses to dorsal raphe stimulation exhibited task uncertainty-dependent variations (Cazettes et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Other modulatory systems (e.g., serotonergic and cholinergic) may modulate the pupil–LC coupling in a dynamic manner.
source: Thus, it is also possible that other modulatory systems (e.g., serotonergic and cholinergic, Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003) modulate the pupil–LC coupling in a dynamic manner.
evidence: Presented as a possible explanation with citation to prior research.

claim: In Hit trials, the latency of LC responses to tone onset was 0.064 ± 0.005 s.
source: In Hit trials, the latency of LC responses to tone onset was 0.064 ± 0.005 s, and to whisker stimulation onset was 0.111 ± 0.008 s, and the reaction time (first lick latency to whisker stimulation onset) of the mice was 0.58 ± 0.03 s.
evidence: Supported by analysis of trial-aligned data.

claim: In Hit trials, the latency of LC responses to whisker stimulation onset was 0.111 ± 0.008 s.
source: In Hit trials, the latency of LC responses to tone onset was 0.064 ± 0.005 s, and to whisker stimulation onset was 0.111 ± 0.008 s, and the reaction time (first lick latency to whisker stimulation onset) of the mice was 0.58 ± 0.03 s.
evidence: Supported by analysis of trial-aligned data.

claim: The reaction time (first lick latency to whisker stimulation onset) of the mice was 0.58 ± 0.03 s.
source: In Hit trials, the latency of LC responses to tone onset was 0.064 ± 0.005 s, and to whisker stimulation onset was 0.111 ± 0.008 s, and the reaction time (first lick latency to whisker stimulation onset) of the mice was 0.58 ± 0.03 s.
evidence: Supported by analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Mean hit rate was 0.52 ± 0.03.
source: A total of 46 recordings from eight mice are reported (mean hit rate: 0.52 ± 0.03; false alarm rate: 0.11 ± 0.02).
evidence: Supported by behavioral performance data.

claim: False alarm rate was 0.11 ± 0.02.
source: A total of 46 recordings from eight mice are reported (mean hit rate: 0.52 ± 0.03; false alarm rate: 0.11 ± 0.02).
